lesson.title: Products with Many Factors: Log Differentiation Earns Its Keep
lesson.summary: The ordinary product rule handles two factors just fine, but multiplying three or more functions together the traditional way multiplies the bookkeeping just as fast; logarithmic differentiation turns that multiplication into simple addition.
lesson.body:
The two factor product rule says (uv)' = u'v + uv'. Stretching it to three factors gives (uvw)' = u'vw + uv'w + uvw', and the pattern keeps growing: n factors need n terms, each one missing the derivative of exactly one factor. That formula is completely correct, but it gets easy to drop a term or mismatch a factor, especially once each piece is itself a power of a polynomial.

Logarithmic differentiation, introduced in the previous chapter, sidesteps all of that bookkeeping. Taking the natural log of a product of any number of factors turns the entire right side into a sum, since ln(f1 f2 ... fn) = ln f1 + ln f2 + ... + ln fn, and differentiating a sum just means differentiating each piece separately and adding the results, with no product rule required at any point.

As a worked example, take a product of three factors: y = x^3 (2x+1)^4 (5-x)^2. Step one: ln y = 3 ln x + 4 ln(2x+1) + 2 ln(5-x). Step two: differentiating gives y'/y = 3/x + 4 times 2/(2x+1) + 2 times (-1)/(5-x) = 3/x + 8/(2x+1) - 2/(5-x), where the last term picks up a minus sign from the chain rule since d/dx(5-x) = -1. Step three and four: solving for y' and substituting back gives y' = x^3(2x+1)^4(5-x)^2 times [3/x + 8/(2x+1) - 2/(5-x)]. Reaching this with the ordinary product rule would require two separate applications of the two factor rule, each one demanding careful tracking of which factor is held fixed; the log version needed only three easy one variable derivatives, added together.

This same idea extends smoothly to factors that are quotients or contain radicals, since the log turns division into subtraction and roots into fractional exponents that come down as simple multipliers. The next chapter pushes the technique further, applying it to a single expression raised to a complicated power rather than several expressions multiplied together.
